chapters.title: Prologue: The Eye and the Mists

scenes.title: The Morning Walk
scenes.subtitle: Neverwinter — Before Dawn

narrationBlocks.text: The city of Neverwinter stands proudly on the Sword Coast, west and north of Dessarin Valley. You know this city — its cobblestones worn smooth by generations of boots and cart wheels, the iron tang of forge smoke that bleeds into the morning air before the sun clears the eastern wall, the ceaseless rhythm of the harbor where rigging clinks against masts like wind chimes made of chain. Fifty years ago, Mount Hotenow nearly leveled everything. Today the scars hide beneath new stone and fresh mortar, and Neverwinter calls itself rebuilt. Most days, you'd believe it.

But this morning, something is wrong. The fog came in before dawn — not the usual sea fog that rolls along the harbor and burns off by midmorning. This is heavier. Lower. Slower. It gathers at the base of buildings like something spilled and never cleaned up, sitting in the gutters and pooling around the foundations of things with a patience that weather doesn't have. The usual view north toward the docks — the forest of masts, the painted hulls, the harbor master's flags — is gone. Just a flat wall of grey where the world should be. Even the ravens on the city walls have gone quiet, hunched on their ledges with their heads tucked, as though they've decided today is not a day for flying.

The air tastes flat. Not cold, not warm — neutral in a way that air shouldn't be. Your footsteps sound close and intimate on the damp cobblestones, but the rest of the city — the distant clang of the Protector's Enclave bell tower, the early shouts of dock workers, the creak of shop signs — all of it sounds impossibly far away, like a memory of a city rather than the city itself.

PACING: This scene should take no more than five minutes. You are establishing mood, not mystery. The fog is not a puzzle to solve — it is a feeling. One atmospheric beat per character, then move to the keep.

Deliver one line per character as they walk separately through the city toward the keep. Go around the table:

• Fighter / Martial: 'The city guard at the Dolphin Bridge checkpoint doesn't make eye contact as you pass. His knuckles are white on the haft of his spear, and he's facing inward, toward the city — not outward, the way guards face.'

• Druid / Ranger: 'The ravens that nest on the harbor warehouses are gone. Not sleeping — gone. Every ledge is empty. You've walked past three separate bird nests on your way here, and every one of them is abandoned. Even the pigeons. You have never seen Neverwinter without pigeons.'

• Warlock / Sorcerer: 'You can feel the ambient magic of the city — the enchanted street lamps, the minor wards on shop doors, the faint hum of the Cloak Tower's defenses in the distance — and it feels thin. Stretched. Like a drumhead pulled too tight, vibrating at a frequency just below hearing.'

• Rogue / Bard: 'The morning market vendors are setting up their stalls in the Protector's Enclave, arranging fish and bread and winter apples in neat rows. Every single one of them is looking over their shoulder. Not at anything specific. Just — behind.'

• Cleric / Paladin: 'You said your morning prayer at the usual hour. The words came easily. The response did not. Where your deity normally answers with warmth — that familiar pressure in the chest, the quiet certainty that you are heard — there was nothing. Not absence. Silence. The difference matters.'

A messenger finds each of you before the morning bells. Different streets, different moments, but the same urgency. The boy is young — twelve, maybe thirteen — and moves through the fog with the practiced confidence of someone who has memorized every shortcut in this city. The seal on the folded note is unmistakable: the Lord Protector's sigil, pressed deep into black wax that's still warm. The note inside is five words:

'Your presence is required immediately.'
The boy is gone before you can ask a question. You look up from the note, and the space where he was standing is just fog, settling back into place like water filling a footprint.

IF PLAYERS INVESTIGATE THE FOG:

DC 13 Nature or Survival (Passive counts if 13+):
SUCCESS: This fog is not natural. Natural fog has direction, temperature gradient, moisture — it smells of salt or minerals depending on its source. This has none of those properties. It isn't moving toward or away from anything. It is simply present, like it grew here overnight from the stone itself.

DC 14 Arcana (only if someone actively probes with magic):
SUCCESS: There is a planar signature in the air — faint, ancient, and entirely unlike any local enchantment. This is not weather magic or a hex. It carries the resonance of somewhere else. Somewhere that has been watching for a very long time.

FAILURE on either: 'It looks wrong to you, but you can't say why. Your instincts whisper — your training offers nothing.'

choices.consequence: You pull your cloak tighter and make your way through the fog-choked streets. The keep's silhouette emerges from the grey like the prow of a ship.
You spend a few minutes studying the fog — probing it with senses or spells — before the note's urgency wins. The fog offers nothing but patience. The keep awaits.

scenes.dmNotes:
The fog is not solvable yet. It cannot be dispersed by mundane wind, Gust, or any spell below 4th level. If someone tries to backtrack: the street behind looks identical to the street ahead. If a druid wild shapes into a bird: the fog goes up — they cannot find the top. If someone lights a torch: it illuminates 5 feet, no more.

The goal of this scene is a single feeling: something is already wrong, and no one can explain it.

scenes.title: The Lord Protector
scenes.subtitle: Neverember's Keep — Private Study

narrationBlocks.text: Neverember's Keep rises from the fog like a clenched fist of grey stone and iron-banded oak. The banners of the Lord Protector — silver and blue, the Neverwinter crest — hang limp from the battlements. No wind to stir them. The guards at the main gate wave you through without the usual credential check, which is unusual enough to notice. The one on the right has the careful blankness of a man who has been told to expect you and to ask no questions about why.

Inside, the keep is quieter than it should be. No petitioners shuffling in the entrance hall. No clerks arguing over tax ledgers in the corridor. The usual bustle of governance — the papers, the runners, the bureaucratic friction of a city being run — is absent. Your footsteps echo on stone floors that are usually crowded enough to muffle them. An aide appears from a side passage, nods once, and leads you up a tight spiral staircase to a second-floor room you've never been invited into. The Lord Protector's private study. The door closes behind you with a click that sounds deliberately final.

The study is smaller than you expected. Oak-paneled walls. A window overlooking the harbor — or what would be the harbor, if the fog hadn't swallowed it. A heavy desk dominates the center, buried under maps — detailed cartographic work annotated in a crisp, military hand, with clusters of red marking pins driven into the western ruins district. The seal on each map is military, not civic. Whatever this is, it hasn't gone through the usual channels. A crystal decanter of amber liquor sits on a side table, poured but untouched — the glass beside it catching what little light makes it through the fog-dimmed window.

Dagult Neverember stands behind the desk. He is a big man — broad across the shoulders, with a statesman's bearing and a merchant's eyes. His dark hair is shot through with silver at the temples, and his beard is trimmed close and going grey in a way that makes him look more like a retired general than a politician. He is not sitting. He has not invited you to sit. He is looking at each of you in turn — not threatening, not aggressive. Assessing. This is a man deciding, in real time, how much to trust you with.
He lets the silence hold for exactly one beat too long. A politician's trick — or a commander's. He wants you slightly off-balance before he begins.

Neverwinter doesn't have a formal militia. What it has is people I trust to handle things that need handling without leaving a paper trail for every clerk and council member in this building to gossip about. That is the specific reason each of you is in this room right now.
narrationBlocks.speaker: Lord Neverember
narrationBlocks.emotion: Low, measured — he speaks like a man who runs a city and is accustomed to being listened to without raising his voice

narrationBlocks.text: For several months, we've been tracking suspicious activity in the western ruins. Organized gatherings in the old catacomb network beneath the burial district. Hooded figures. Underground rituals. The kind of thing that could be nothing — zealots playing at religion in an abandoned sewer — or the kind of thing that gets people killed in their beds if we ignore it long enough.
narrationBlocks.speaker: Lord Neverember
narrationBlocks.emotion: He moves to the map and taps a cluster of red pins — each one driven deep into the parchment, the wood beneath pocked with small holes from being placed, removed, and replaced

narrationBlocks.text: I have two investigators working the surface — a pair of siblings named Kevori and Delvin Fearnehart. Good people. Discreet. They've identified entry points and mapped the above-ground approach, but they haven't gone in. Two scouts in a catacomb full of whatever this is — that's reconnaissance, not resolution. I need resolution.
narrationBlocks.speaker: Lord Neverember
narrationBlocks.emotion: He turns from the map to face you directly — the first real eye contact, and it is uncomfortably direct

narrationBlocks.text: The city pays well for capable people. And it pays more for information than for bodies. If there are people down there, I want them alive. Every cultist you bring me breathing is worth ten gold to the city. Their leader, if there is one — twenty-five.
narrationBlocks.speaker: Lord Neverember
narrationBlocks.emotion: He opens a desk drawer with a brass key from his pocket, pulls out a sealed leather envelope, and slides it across the desk — 100 gp advance, the weight of it landing with authority

narrationBlocks.text: I'm told you're the right people for this. Prove it.
narrationBlocks.speaker: Lord Neverember
narrationBlocks.emotion: Flat, direct — the pitch is over, the contract is on the table, and he is waiting to see what you do with it

narrationBlocks.text:
LORD NEVEREMBER — CHARACTER NOTES:

Dagult Neverember is nicknamed 'Dagger' by those who know him well — not because he's violent, but because he is precise, pragmatic, and cuts straight to the point. He rebuilt Neverwinter from ruins using his own fortune, mercenaries, and political cunning. He was ousted as Open Lord of Waterdeep for embezzlement and carries that wound quietly.

He is not a villain. He is not a hero. He is a man who runs a city the way a merchant runs a business — with an eye on the ledger and a willingness to make ugly decisions if the numbers demand it. He respects competence over title, results over promises.

He does NOT get sentimental. If players with family ties push the personal angle, his response is: 'That's exactly why I called you. I know what you're capable of. I also know you won't be careless.' This is confidence, not warmth. Do not let him be warm.

NEVEREMBER DIALOGUE TREE — Use whichever questions the players ask. If they don't ask, he volunteers nothing extra.

'What kind of cult?' → He pauses one beat. 'The name the Whispered One has come up in two separate intelligence reports from two separate sources who did not know each other existed. Whether that is a title, a deity, or someone's idea of a dramatic pseudonym — I need you to determine.'

'Why us? Why not the City Watch?' → 'Because the Watch leaks like a fishing net. Because rumors in this city travel faster than plague. Because I cannot afford a public panic over something that might be nothing — or might be significantly worse than nothing. I need people who can work quietly and come back with answers, not questions.'

'What do we do exactly?' → 'Infiltrate. Observe. Identify leadership. And bring them in alive if you can manage it. Ten gold per breathing cultist. Twenty-five for whoever is running the show. The envelope on the desk is your advance — one hundred gold, split however you see fit.'

'When do we go?' → 'Not tonight. Go downstairs. Meet the Fearneharts. They know the surface layout — entry points, patrol timing, the geography. Together, you plan the approach. You go in tomorrow at first dark.' He glances toward the fog-dimmed window. 'Assuming we have a tomorrow that resembles today.'

'What about the fog?' → His eyes flick to the window. For one breath — just one — something crosses his face that isn't quite fear. Its well-behaved cousin, maybe. Concern wearing a diplomatic mask. 'I know about the fog. I have reports about the fog. I do not know what it means. If what is happening underground is connected to what is happening in my sky — I need that information yesterday.'

'Can we prepare? Do we have time?' → 'Take what you need from the city armory — within reason. Tell the quartermaster Neverember sent you. Meet the Fearneharts downstairs when you're ready.'

DC 12 Insight (optional — if anyone studies Neverember while he speaks):

SUCCESS: His jaw is clenched slightly harder than his tone suggests. He is controlling something — not deception exactly, but omission. He knows more than he is sharing and has decided to parcel it out based on what you bring back. He is also watching your reactions to his words more carefully than a man who is merely assigning a job needs to. Something about this is personal to him, though he would never admit it.

FAILURE: He reads as entirely straightforward — a practical man hiring practical people for a practical problem.

DC 13 Investigation (if someone studies the maps on his desk):

SUCCESS: The red pins form two clear clusters — one around a cooper's workshop on Saltriver Lane, another near an old sewer access point in the western ruins. But there is a third pin, alone, further east than the others — near the old Illusk quarter ruins. It has been placed, removed, and replaced multiple times. The wood beneath it is pocked with dozens of tiny holes. Whatever is at that location, Neverember has been thinking about it obsessively.

FAILURE: The maps show the western ruins. Nothing else stands out.

choices.consequence: You take the envelope. One hundred gold, heavy in the hand. The aide reappears to lead you downstairs.
You push, but Neverember is a wall. 'The Fearneharts have the operational details. I have a city to keep from panicking. Go.' His tone leaves no room for negotiation.

entities.name: Lord Dagult Neverember
entities.description: Lord Protector of Neverwinter. Tall, broad-shouldered, dark hair silvering at the temples, close-trimmed grey beard. Nicknamed 'Dagger' for his pragmatism. Rebuilt Neverwinter from the ashes of Mount Hotenow with his own fortune. Ousted from Waterdeep. Not a villain, not a hero — a man who runs a city like a business and makes the ugly decisions the ledger demands. Respects competence. Does not do warmth.

scenes.dmNotes:
Neverember should feel like the most competent person in the room — and he knows it. He doesn't posture. He doesn't threaten. He states facts and waits for you to be smart enough to act on them. If a player makes a joke, he waits it out with the polite patience of a man who has attended a thousand diplomatic dinners. If someone demonstrates genuine insight — especially about the fog — allow him exactly one beat of honest reaction before the mask comes back.

The envelope contains 100 gp. This is the advance. The bounty is separate: 10 gp per living cultist, 25 gp for the leader.

scenes.title: The Fearnehart Briefing
scenes.subtitle: Neverember's Keep — Anteroom

narrationBlocks.text: One floor down, past the garrison hall where off-duty soldiers play cards with the distracted energy of people who know something is wrong but haven't been told what — a small anteroom. Rough fieldstone walls. A single guttering oil lamp. A table that's seen better decades, its surface scarred with knife marks and ring stains, now covered by a hand-drawn sketch of the western ruins district, held flat by a pair of daggers driven point-first into opposite corners.

Two people wait. The woman stands over the map with the straight-backed composure of someone who is always ready to leave a room quickly. Dark hair pulled tight at her jaw. Light leather armor that's been maintained with the particular care of someone who has needed it to save their life more than once — the stitching repaired in three places, the buckles oiled, the edges worn soft from use. Her face is lean, watchful, and gives away exactly nothing she doesn't choose to give.

Beside her, leaning against the wall with his arms crossed and his weight on one hip, is a younger man — her brother, clearly, though where she is composed he is casual. He has the easy, comfortable posture of someone who is either genuinely relaxed in all situations or very good at pretending to be. Sandy-brown hair that could use a cut. A quick, lopsided smile that arrives before you've finished introducing yourself. He looks like someone who could disappear in a crowd of three and reappear behind you without you noticing the transition.
Kevori Fearnehart. This is my brother Delvin. The Lord Protector said you'd be joining us. He didn't say how many.
narrationBlocks.speaker: Kevori Fearnehart
narrationBlocks.emotion: Polite, efficient — she is already measuring you. Her eyes check your weapons, your armor, your hands, your eyes, in that order. This is someone who has learned to assess threat before she assesses character.

narrationBlocks.text: Four months of watching and the best part? Nothing's tried to eat us yet. That's a win in this city.
narrationBlocks.speaker: Delvin Fearnehart
narrationBlocks.emotion: He pushes off the wall with a lopsided nod, warm and easy — the kind of charm that comes naturally to people who genuinely like other people

narrationBlocks.text: He's already looking at whatever weapon the nearest character is carrying — not with threat, but with the idle, genuine curiosity of someone who notices things for a living. If you have something unusual, he'll comment. If you don't, he'll ask what you prefer and why, with the honest interest of someone building a mental file that might save his life later.

DELVIN — THE MOST IMPORTANT NPC IN THE PROLOGUE:

Delvin Fearnehart is going to die. This is not optional. While the party spends what feels like 2-3 days inside Death House, approximately three weeks pass in Neverwinter. During that time, Delvin goes into the catacombs alone to look for the party. He infiltrates the cult. He gets caught. He dies.

When the party escapes Death House and returns to Neverwinter, they will find Kevori screaming in agony over his body in a rain-soaked alley — his grey cult robe torn, a desiccated eyeball rolling from his open palm. That is the inciting incident of Nest of the Eldritch Eye.

That moment will land like a hammer or fall flat depending entirely on what you do right now. You have five to ten minutes. Make the players like him. Make them want to buy him a drink. Make them remember his name.

He cracks small jokes. He asks genuine questions. He makes self-deprecating asides. He has a tell — when he's actually worried about something, he fidgets with a leather cord bracelet on his left wrist. He never draws attention to it. But if a player notices, it's a detail that will haunt them later when Kevori is holding his cold wrist and the bracelet is still there.

Cult gatherings beneath the western ruins. Four months. We tracked them to an entrance — old drainage tunnel behind Hendrick's cooperage on Saltriver Lane. We found it eight weeks ago when a street collapsed and opened a sinkhole right next to the workshop. Haven't gone in.
narrationBlocks.speaker: Kevori Fearnehart
narrationBlocks.emotion: Briefing-mode — she has said these words before, possibly rehearsed them. Her tone is flat from repetition, but her eyes are not flat. She watches the party while she speaks, checking whether they are listening or performing listening.

narrationBlocks.text: Grey robes, not black. They don't cause trouble topside — whatever they're doing, it's underground. They come in groups of four or five after midnight. Covered lanterns. They don't speak above a whisper. Haven't noticed us. We want to keep it that way.
narrationBlocks.speaker: Delvin Fearnehart
narrationBlocks.emotion: He taps a spot on the map as he speaks — the drainage tunnel entrance. His finger is ink-stained. He draws maps for a living.

narrationBlocks.text:
FEARNEHART DIALOGUE TREE — Let the players drive the conversation. If they ask nothing, Kevori offers the plan unprompted.

'What do you know about the Whispered One?' → Delvin glances at Kevori. She gives a micro-nod — barely visible, the kind of permission that comes from years of working together. Then Delvin: 'Name came up twice. Once from a drunk river courier who definitely didn't mean to say it — we were buying him drinks and he let it slip between his fourth and fifth ale. Once carved into a wall in the lower catacomb passage we mapped from above. Could be a title. Could be a god. Could be their password for the door.' A beat. He fidgets with the bracelet on his left wrist. 'Didn't feel like nothing, though.'

'Have you been inside at all?' → Kevori, immediately: 'No.' Delvin: 'Kevori says no. So — no.' A beat and a crooked grin. 'She's usually right about these things. It's annoying.'

'What's down there?' → Kevori: 'We don't know. We've heard chanting twice — low, rhythmic. It stopped both times within a few minutes. We counted eleven distinct voices once. We may have miscounted — echo plays tricks in those tunnels.'

'What's the plan?' → Kevori: 'Walk the western ruins with us tonight. Get eyes on the terrain. The streets, the approaches, the exits. Nobody goes in yet. Tomorrow at first dark, you go in and we hold the surface point as your fallback. If you're not out in four hours, we go to Neverember.'

'Can't you do this yourselves?' → Kevori: 'Two scouts in a catacomb full of cultists? We can map it. We can count them. But if it goes wrong underground, nobody pulls us out. Neverember wants results, not just intelligence.'

'Are you coming with us underground?' → Kevori: 'We hold the surface. That's the plan.' Delvin, quieter, looking at the party rather than his sister: 'We'll be there. At the entrance. Waiting.' He makes a small gesture — informal, somehow reassuring. Like a promise between strangers that might actually mean something.

'Ready to go?' → Delvin rolls up the hand-drawn map and hands it to whoever seems like the planner in the group. 'Bring it back. I spent an hour on that and I only have the one.' He is joking. Almost certainly.

DC 12 Insight (optional — after any significant interaction with either sibling):

SUCCESS: Kevori is protective of Delvin in a way she is actively trying not to show. She positions herself slightly between him and the party — not blocking, but close enough to react. She is assigning this operation with his safety in mind as much as the mission's success: she wants him on the surface, away from whatever is underground, and she has structured the plan to ensure that without making it obvious.

Delvin knows this. He is gently, patiently tolerant of it — the way younger siblings tolerate older siblings who have been protecting them since childhood and probably always will.

FAILURE: They read as professional, competent, and well-coordinated. Standard investigative partnership.

Kevori gives you the rest of what they have — entry timing, the general layout visible from the sinkhole, one hand-drawn sketch of the surface approach that Delvin clearly spent real time on. The lines are careful. The distances are annotated. There's a small compass rose in the corner, unnecessarily beautiful, drawn by someone who takes quiet pride in doing things well.
Twenty-minute walk to the western district. Let's go.
narrationBlocks.speaker: Delvin Fearnehart
narrationBlocks.emotion: He rolls his shoulders, cracks his neck with practiced ease, and moves toward the door with the comfortable urgency of someone who would rather be doing than planning. He glances at the window and his expression flickers — just for a moment. The fog outside is thicker than it was.

narrationBlocks.text: We might want to stay close. Fog's gotten worse.
narrationBlocks.speaker: Delvin Fearnehart
narrationBlocks.emotion: Quieter now — the joke is gone. He noticed something. He is not going to say what.

choices.consequence: All six of you step out into the fog-choked streets of Neverwinter. The keep's torches vanish behind you in three steps.
You press for details, but Kevori shakes her head. 'Better to show you than tell you. Let's walk.' Delvin is already at the door.

entities.name: Kevori Fearnehart
entities.description: Human scout. Lean, dark hair pulled tight, light leather armor worn soft from use. Polite but efficient — answers questions directly, doesn't volunteer extra. Protective of Delvin in ways she tries to hide. She assesses threats before she assesses character. Neutral good.

entities.name: Delvin Fearnehart
entities.description: Human investigator. Younger, sandy-brown hair, lopsided smile. Easy manner, genuine warmth. Good at disappearing in crowds. Draws maps with unnecessary care. Fidgets with a leather cord bracelet when worried. Neutral good. He is going to die during the party's absence, and this is the last time they will see him alive.

scenes.dmNotes:
Budget ten minutes for this. The only goal is to make Delvin feel like a person. Not a questgiver, not a plot device — a person with habits and warmth and a sister who worries about him. Everything that follows — his death, Kevori's grief, the eyeball rolling from his palm — is built on what you do in this room.

Kevori delivers facts. Delvin makes you care about the facts.

scenes.title: The Mists Take Them
scenes.subtitle: Neverwinter Streets — The Walk West

narrationBlocks.text: All six of you leave the keep together — the four of you, Kevori, and Delvin — walking west through the city toward the ruins district. The fog has thickened considerably while you were inside, and within a block of the keep, you can no longer see its walls behind you. The torches mounted on the gatehouse — bright enough to read by when you arrived — are orange smears that fade to nothing in the time it takes to blink.

The city that greeted you this morning has changed. The streets you know are still beneath your feet — the same cobblestones, the same gutter channels, the same iron sewer grates — but the fog has become something else entirely. It doesn't move the way fog moves. It doesn't drift on thermals or thin at crossings where the wind should cut through. It simply is — filling every gap, every alley, every space between buildings with patient, absolute grey, turning a city you have memorized into a place you have never been.

Landmarks dissolve. A bakery you've passed a hundred times — the one with the copper rooster sign that squeaks in the wind — the sign is gone. Not fallen. Not broken off. Just absent, as though it was never hung. A fountain in a small courtyard — you can hear the water but you can't find the basin. Delvin points at a side street that should lead to Helmsman's Row, but the alley stretches too long and too narrow and the far end isn't visible. It looks like a throat.
...How long have we been walking?
narrationBlocks.speaker: Kevori Fearnehart
narrationBlocks.emotion: She glances over her shoulder. For the first time since you met her — the first crack in that composure. She knows exactly how long a twenty-minute walk should take. It has been longer than that.

narrationBlocks.text: And then, between one step and the next, you realize they're gone. Not dramatically — not yanked away, not swallowed by a flash of magic. Kevori was beside you. Now that space is fog. Delvin was two steps to the left and slightly behind. Fog. No sound of their footsteps stopping. No cry of surprise. No rustle of movement. The spaces they occupied simply filled with grey and forgot they were ever there.
Kevori?
narrationBlocks.speaker: You
narrationBlocks.emotion: Your voice sounds small and close, like you are speaking into a cupped hand

narrationBlocks.text: Nothing. The fog doesn't even echo. It absorbs your voice the way a pillow absorbs a scream.
Delvin?
narrationBlocks.speaker: You
narrationBlocks.emotion: Louder now — and the loudness costs you something, because the silence that follows is heavier than the silence before

narrationBlocks.text: The fog doesn't answer. It just stands there. Patient.

You keep walking. There is nothing else to do. The cobblestones continue beneath your feet, but the gaps between them are filling with something that isn't mud and isn't moss — something dark and glistening, like the ground itself is sweating. There is no sun. There are no street sounds. There is no wind. You have been walking for what feels like twenty minutes, then thirty, then an hour. The city you grew up in — or chose, or fled to — is gone. You are walking through the memory of a place, and the memory is fading.

PACING: Three minutes of narration, maximum. This scene should feel disorienting, not tedious. Momentum is everything — do not let the players stop to deliberate. The mists move faster than discussion.

IF PLAYERS TRY SPELLS OR ABILITIES:
• Detect Magic: Nothing registers. This predates mortal spellcraft.
• Dispel Magic / Remove Curse: No effect.
• Light cantrip or torch: Illuminates 5 feet. Beyond that, absolute grey.
• Misty Step or short-range teleportation: They arrive at the same spot. The fog ignores planar shortcuts.
• Holding hands or roping together: Works — they arrive together. Good instinct.
• Attempting to go backward: The street behind is identical to the street ahead. There is no 'back.'

VECNA'S WHISPERS IN THE MIST — These four beats should be spaced across the walk. Don't cluster them. Drop one between player discussions or decisions. Each is a single moment, not a setpiece:

1. THE SILHOUETTE — At the very edge of visibility — ten feet, maybe less — a figure. Tall. Thin. Perfectly still. By the time anyone's eyes focus on it properly, it isn't there. No sound of movement. No footprints in the glistening cobblestones where it stood.

2. THE WHISPER (highest Passive Perception only) — Against the total silence, barely audible: a single syllable. Not a word. The beginning of one, cut off. It comes from the left, or behind, or from inside the back of their skull. The other characters heard nothing. If the player asks 'what did it say?' — 'You're not sure it said anything. But you're not sure it didn't.'

3. THE HAND (pick one character — preferably one who would be deeply unsettled) — They glance at their own hand while walking. For one breath — just one — the faint outline of an eye is visible beneath the skin of their palm. Not drawn on it. Beneath it. Pressed against the underside of their skin from the inside, as if something within is looking out. Then it is gone. Their hand looks normal. It didn't hurt. They felt nothing except the sudden, absolute certainty that they were being watched by something that was already inside them.

4. THE RAVEN — A single black raven lands on the cobblestones a few feet ahead. It looks at each of them in turn — not with animal curiosity, but with appraisal. Deliberate, intelligent, assessing. It opens its beak without making a sound, holds that silent pose for three heartbeats, then launches straight up and vanishes into the fog above. Ravens in Faerûn carry no inherent supernatural meaning. This will feel like it does anyway.

WHAT HAPPENED TO THE FEARNEHARTS:

The mists took only the party. Kevori and Delvin arrive at the western ruins a few minutes later — alone, disoriented, unsure what happened. They search. They wait. Eventually, they get to work.

While the party spends what feels like 2-3 days in Death House, approximately three weeks pass in Neverwinter. During that time, Delvin — frustrated, worried, feeling responsible — attempts the catacomb infiltration alone. He puts on a grey robe. He learns the phrase 'Hail the Undying.' He gets inside. And he does not come back out.

When the party escapes Death House, the mists will deposit them at the gates of Neverwinter. Kevori will be screaming over Delvin's body. A desiccated eyeball will roll from his open palm. The leather cord bracelet will still be on his wrist. Nest of the Eldritch Eye begins exactly as written.

DC 13 Constitution Saving Throw — Call this as vertigo hits. Tell players to roll and note their results:

FAILURE: The character staggers forward out of the fog on their hands and knees, palms in cold mud, nauseous. Disadvantage on their first ability check in the new location.

SUCCESS: The vertigo is severe but manageable. They land on their feet — barely. The world tilts and then snaps back into place with the sickening lurch of a dream where you miss a step on the stairs.

And then — as suddenly as it began — the world snaps back. Not the world you know. A different one. Cold ground. Different air. Different sky. The fog is still there, but it's behind you now — a wall, not a presence. You are nowhere you recognize.

choices.consequence: The ground is gravel, not cobblestone. The air smells of wet earth and old wood. The fog has stepped back — but only just.

scenes.dmNotes: This is the abduction. Play it with momentum — no stopping, no deliberation. The mists move faster than player agency, and that loss of control is intentional. Players should feel like something immeasurably large just reached down and picked them up. The helplessness is the point. It will only happen once. Make it count.

scenes.title: Arrival in Barovia
scenes.subtitle: Village of Barovia — The Dead Street

narrationBlocks.text: The ground has changed. Not cobblestone — gravel. Loose, cold, chewed up by wheels and weather and what might be decades of neglect. The air is different too — colder, heavier, carrying the smell of old wood and earth and, beneath those things, something older. Something that has been decaying for so long it has stopped smelling like rot and started smelling like stone. Like geology. Like time itself going sour.

The fog has thinned — not dissipated, just pulled back, held at the edges of wherever you are like a curtain drawn aside just enough to show you what's behind it. And what's behind it is a village. Tall stone houses rise on either side of a narrow street, their walls stained dark with damp, their windows either shuttered or boarded over from the inside. A few shops — closed, locked, signs faded to illegibility. A tavern with a heavy oak door and iron bands, shut tight, its windows dark. No smoke from any chimney. No light from any window. No sound from any door.

Silence. Not the absence of sound — silence, the active, oppressive kind, the kind that has weight and temperature and the patient malevolence of something that is listening to you as carefully as you are listening to it. The only thing you can hear is your own breathing, and it sounds very loud, and you wish it wouldn't.

PLAYER MOMENT: Go around the table. Ask each player simply: 'What is the first thing your character does?' Note whether they draw a weapon, look for danger, try to orient themselves, look for the others, pray, or try to cast a spell. These instincts tell you who these characters are. After everyone has had their moment — continue.

The village stretches in both directions, but nowhere invites exploration. The houses nearest you are dark and closed and have the particular stillness of places that have been empty for a long time — not abandoned in haste but vacated slowly, deliberately, the way people leave a place they know is dying. Curtains hang in fragments behind cracked glass. A child's wooden horse sits on a windowsill three houses down, bleached grey by weather, the paint worn to nothing by a wind that isn't blowing.

IF PLAYERS EXPLORE THE OTHER HOUSES:

Let them try. Every house they approach shows the same thing — boarded windows, locked doors, the silence of a place that has given up. If they force a door (DC 12 Athletics or DC 10 with tools), they find dust, cold hearths, furniture draped in cloth that disintegrates at a touch. No food. No bodies. No signs of violence — just the slow, thorough emptying of a life.

But the fog notices. Each time they approach a house that isn't the Death House, the mist at the edges of the village tightens — imperceptibly at first, then obviously. By the time they've investigated two or three buildings, the fog has swallowed the houses at both ends of the street. Where a moment ago there were a dozen visible buildings, now there are eight. Then six. Then four. The village is shrinking around them, house by house, as though the fog is erasing everything that isn't relevant to where they are supposed to go.

If they persist: the fog continues closing until only one building remains — the tall brick row house at the end of the street. The one with the gated portico. The one that is expecting them.

DC 14 Arcana, History, or Religion — Anyone who tries to identify where they are:

SUCCESS: The ambient magic here is thick and oppressive — not the structured, layered enchantment of a city ward, but something deeper, older, woven into the ground itself like roots. A character who has studied planar cosmology would recognize this as a Domain of Dread — a pocket dimension, sealed from the outside by a consciousness so powerful it has become geography. A cleric would feel their deity connection muffled — not severed, but distant. Like calling through a closed door in a house where no one answers.

FAILURE: The magic is too foreign. Nothing in the Forgotten Realms feels like this. Your training has no category for it.

FOG BOUNDARY: If players attempt to leave the village by walking into the fog:

The fog wall is solidly cold — not weather-cold but absence-cold, the cold of a space that does not contain heat because it does not contain anything. Stepping into it is like stepping into standing water that goes to your chest in a single stride. DC 15 Constitution save or take 1d10 cold damage and 1 level of exhaustion. It does not burn. It does not shock. It simply refuses, with the gentle, implacable patience of something that has all the time in the world.

A soft whimpering draws your attention back to the street. Two children stand in the middle of the empty road, thirty feet ahead. The older one — a girl, about ten — has her arm around the younger, a boy of maybe seven who clutches a stuffed doll to his chest and shakes with quiet, hiccupping sobs. He presses his face into her side. She holds him with one arm and looks up at you with eyes that are far, far too composed for a child standing alone in a dead village at the end of the world.
There's a monster in our house.
narrationBlocks.speaker: Rose
narrationBlocks.emotion: Quiet. Steady. The way a child speaks when they have been scared for so long that fear has become furniture — it is simply there, taking up space, and they have learned to move around it

narrationBlocks.text: She points. At the end of the street — the only building the fog has not yet touched — a tall brick row house. Three stories, maybe four. A gated portico, the iron gate slightly ajar, hinges dark with rust. Dark windows that reflect nothing. The houses on either side of it are boarded up and sagging, as though even the neighboring buildings are trying to lean away from it.

ROSE AND THORN — CRITICAL NPC INFORMATION:

• Rose (Rosavalda Durst), age 10. Girl. Composed, protective, the older sibling who has been holding things together.
• Thorn (Thornboldt Durst), age 7. Boy. Clutches a stuffed doll. Tearful, quiet, stays pressed against Rose's side.

BOTH ARE ILLUSIONS created by the house to lure adventurers inside. They do not know they are illusions. They will not enter the house — they vanish if attacked or if someone attempts to force them inside.

Their real skeletons are in the attic (Area 20), in a locked children's bedroom. They starved to death after their parents locked them in to 'protect' them from the basement.

The party will find those skeletons. The clothes on the skeletons will match what the children are wearing now. Thorn's skeleton will be cradling the same stuffed doll. Let that detail do its work.

ROSE & THORN DIALOGUE — Let the players ask. Rose does most of the talking. Thorn rarely speaks — he watches from behind his sister with wide, wet eyes.

'What kind of monster?' → Rose: 'We don't know what it looks like. We hear it at night — terrible howls from the basement. Mama and Papa keep it locked down there.' She swallows. 'They said they'd take care of it.'

'Where are your parents?' → Rose: 'Inside. They told us to wait out here. They said they'd come get us when it was safe.' She doesn't look convinced. She looks like she has been telling herself this for a very long time.

'Anyone else inside?' → Rose: 'Walter — our baby brother. He's in the nursery on the third floor. He can't come down by himself.' She believes this entirely. It is not true. The nursery crib contains a bundle wrapped in a black shroud. Inside the bundle is nothing.

'Come inside with us?' → Rose shakes her head firmly, pulling Thorn closer. 'Not until the monster is gone.' She will not be persuaded. She cannot enter. She is not real enough to walk through the door.

'What's your name?' → 'I'm Rose. This is my brother Thorn.' She says it simply, as though it is the most normal introduction in the world. As though anything about this is normal.

'How long have you been out here?' → She hesitates. Her composure flickers for the first time — a frown, confusion, the particular frustration of trying to remember something that should be easy. 'I... I don't remember. It feels like a long time.' Thorn makes a small sound against her side. She pulls him closer and doesn't answer again.

The row house waits at the end of the street. The iron gate is open. The door beyond it is closed but not locked — you can see it from here, the latch resting in its cradle, not seated. The house is not locked. The house has never been locked. The house has been open this entire time, the way a mouth is open before it speaks. Or before it bites.

choices.consequence: You walk through the iron gate. It shrieks on its hinges — the first real sound in this village. The oaken doors beyond yield without resistance, swinging inward like the house has been expecting you.

You investigate the surrounding buildings. The fog tightens with each step away from the house. One by one, the other houses vanish into grey. The message is clear: there is only one place you are meant to go.

entities.name: Rose (Rosavalda Durst)
entities.description: Ten years old. Illusion outside the house, ghost inside, skeleton in the attic. Composed, protective of Thorn, the older sibling who has been holding things together long after things fell apart. She believes her parents are inside fixing the monster problem. She does not know she is dead.

entities.name: Thorn (Thornboldt Durst)
entities.description: Seven years old. Illusion outside the house, ghost inside, skeleton in the attic. Clutches a stuffed doll. Tearful, quiet, rarely speaks. Stays pressed against Rose. The doll will be in the skeleton's arms when the party finds them.

scenes.dmNotes:
This is the moment. Everything before this was setup — the fog, the keep, the Fearneharts, the walk. This is where the campaign actually begins: a dead village, two ghost children, and a house that is waiting.

Pace it slowly. Let the silence work. Let the children's composure be more unsettling than any monster. And when the party finally walks through that gate and those oaken doors swing open — hold for one beat. Let them feel the threshold. Let them feel that they are choosing to go inside.

They aren't, of course. The house chose them. But let them feel like they chose.

scenes.title: The Entrance
scenes.subtitle: Death House – Ground Floor, Area 1

narrationBlocks.text: The village street before you is empty. Not the empty of a sleeping town — the empty of abandonment, as though everyone left in a hurry long ago and did not bother to tell the buildings. Most windows are boarded. Most doors are sealed. The fog presses close on all sides, all but the road directly ahead.

And directly ahead: a house. A tall, narrow, three-story brick rowhouse with a jutting attic above. It is the only building in this village with its lights on — faint, orange-yellow, like candlelight behind dirty glass. The windows are not boarded. The iron gate in the stone portico stands slightly, deliberately, ajar.
No wind. The air is absolutely still. And yet the heavy oak doors behind the gate shudder — once — as if settling their weight. As if breathing.

Then you see the children. A boy and an older girl, huddled together in the middle of the street in front of the gate. The boy wears tattered breeches and a dirty blue shirt, clutching a stuffed cloth doll to his chest, tears streaking through filth on his face. The girl holds his hand with both of hers, eyes wide, looking at each of you in the desperate way that children look at adults when they need someone larger to make the terrible thing stop.

There's a monster. In our house. Our mama and papa went to the basement to trap it and they didn't come back and the baby — Walter, our baby brother — he's crying upstairs and we can't go in because of the monster and —
narrationBlocks.speaker: Rose (the older girl)
narrationBlocks.emotion: Terrified, tumbling over words, trying very hard not to cry and failing

narrationBlocks.text: Please. Please help us. We just want to go home.
narrationBlocks.speaker: Thorn (the younger boy)
narrationBlocks.emotion: A whisper. He does not take his eyes off the house.

narrationBlocks.text: Behind them, through the iron gate, the oak doors remain slightly open. Just enough to show darkness inside.

DC 12 Insight — Ask only if players interact with the children:

SUCCESS: Everything about them is right — the emotion, the body language, the desperation. But their clothes are dry. It has been drizzling since you arrived in the village, and they've been standing here. They should be soaked. Also, when the wind doesn't blow, the girl's hair doesn't move either.

FAILURE: They read as two frightened, ordinary children. Your heart probably breaks a little.

DC 14 Investigation — If a player looks at the street around the children:

SUCCESS: There are muddy child-sized footprints on the cobblestones. They lead from the portico gate to where the children stand, then back, then forward again — as if they've been pacing. But there are no footprints that lead away from the house from any other direction. They didn't walk from anywhere else.

CHILDREN MECHANICS — Print this. You will need it:

Rose and Thorn are illusions created by the house. They are bound to lure visitors inside. Despite this, they experience fear and sadness in a completely genuine way — the house shaped them from the real children's last emotional imprints.

• Physical contact: They feel cold and solid. Unnervingly real.
• If attacked or forcibly moved: They vanish — not dramatically, not with a flash. Just not there anymore, mid-step.
• If players try to leave: The girl looks at you with something worse than pleading. 'You can't go. The fog won't let you.' And she's right — the fog closes in behind the party. The only clear path is the door.
• If players enter without the children: The children remain in the street. If players look back, the children are always watching. If the party waves at them from inside, the children wave back.

The children will not answer questions about the cult, the Durst family secrets, or why they are afraid to go in. They know what children know. No more.

FIXNG VECNA HOOK — VECNA SEED (do this subtly, not overtly):

As the party approaches the gate, let one character — ideally whoever seems most perceptive or magically inclined — notice something on the back of the older girl's right hand: a faint pattern, like a birthmark or old ink. It looks like it could be an eye in the center of a palm. She keeps her hand turned inward, but it catches the light for just a moment.

DO NOT point it out explicitly. Do not have an NPC comment on it. Let the player notice or not notice. This is a seed plant. It will matter later.
The iron gate swings the rest of the way open on its own — a slow, rusty creak followed by silence. Through the portico, the oak doors wait. Behind you, the fog tightens.

The portico is stone. Stone columns, an arched ceiling, oil lamps dark in their wall mounts. The gate has a lock but it is open. The oak doors are ajar. There is nothing stopping you from walking in except every instinct in your body.

choices.text: Step Through the Gate and Enter
choices.consequence: You push through the oak doors into the darkness of the foyer.

entities.name: Rose (Rosavalda Durst)
entities.description: Appears as a girl of about 10. An illusion shaped from the memory of the real child. She is genuinely afraid, genuinely loving, and genuinely dead.

entities.name: Thorn (Thornboldt Durst)
entities.description: Appears as a boy of about 7. Clutches a stuffed doll. Will not look directly at the house. Has not let go of his sister's hand since the party arrived.

scenes.dmNotes: THIS IS THE HOOK SCENE. Play the children as genuine, not theatrical. Real children who are terrified do not perform their terror — they get small and quiet and try to hold onto someone bigger. The horror of this scene is NOT the children being scary. It is that they are not scary at all. They are just two kids who are going to ask you to walk into something awful. Give players the moment to ache.

scenes.title: The Main Hall
scenes.subtitle: Ground Floor, Area 2

narrationBlocks.text: The moment the last of you is inside, the oak doors slam. Not swing — slam. The sound of it reverberates through the house like a struck bell and dies not with an echo but with a horrible completeness, as if the house swallowed the sound. You listen for the village. For any sound from outside. There is nothing. The house has sealed.

You are in a wide entry foyer. A sweeping red marble staircase curves upward to your left, its banister polished to a dark gleam that light doesn't quite bounce off the right way. A crystal chandelier hangs above you — unlit but present, hundreds of cut crystals catching your torchlight and throwing it into cold prisms across the floor. The floor itself is inlaid black marble with a family crest at the center: a windmill on a red field, ringed by carved wolves.
The air inside is warmer than outside. Not warm the way a lit hearth makes a room warm. Warm the way a closed space full of old things gets warm — the warmth of preservation. Of things kept too long.

The walls are dark wood paneling carved with scenes of nature — vines and flowers and nymphs in the lower panels, but let your light play across them for a moment longer and the details emerge: the vines are thorned. The flowers are not opening but closing. The nymphs have their mouths open in what might be song or might be screaming, and you cannot quite tell which because the light keeps moving.

DC 10 Perception (Passive check, no roll needed unless passive is under 10):

SUCCESS: There is a faint sound from above. High and pure, almost like a music box — but with the phrasing of a lullaby. It comes in fragments, stopping and starting, as if interrupted by someone crying.

FAILURE: The house is very quiet. Uncomfortably so.

DC 12 Investigation — If players examine the carved wall panels closely:

SUCCESS: The serpents and skulls are there. Woven into the design so naturally that you almost miss them — a coiled serpent hidden at the base of a grapevine, a skull formed by the negative space between two overlapping flowers. Someone designed these very specifically.

DC 14 Investigation — If players examine the family crest on the floor:

SUCCESS: The windmill on the crest is wrong. Standard heraldry shows the sails moving deosil — clockwise. The Durst windmill sails are turning the other way. Against the sun. Against the natural order. A character with religious training might note this as a deliberate inversion — a sign of something that worships in opposition to natural things.

MAIN HALL INTERACTABLES — Keep a note of these:

• DOORS: The front doors are sealed by the house. Any attempt to force them physically: DC 22 Athletics to budge, and they close again the following round. Attacks: the wood bleeds black sap instead of breaking. Spells of 4th level and under do nothing visible. Tell players the house doesn't want them to leave. It's not dramatic — it's just true.

• CHANDELIER: DC 12 Athletics to climb. Can be swung to reach the upper landing without the stairs. Can be dropped on the landing with a DC 15 Strength check — it falls for 4d8 bludgeoning + shattered crystal shards deal 1d4 to everything in 15 feet (DC 12 Dex save for half on the shards).

• ARMOR STAND: A decorative suit of plate with a longsword. The longsword is real and functions normally. The plate is decorative and cannot be worn. The armor does NOT animate here — that happens on the third floor.

• STAIRCASES: The red marble staircase goes up. A narrower service stair is partially visible at the hall's east end. A closed door is visible to the west (Den of Wolves). An archway to the south leads toward dining.

• LULLABY: The sound from above is the Walter illusion. If players ask what it is — it sounds like a baby crying. Then it stops. Then it starts again. They cannot localize it precisely.
Three options forward: a heavy door to the west, an archway to the south, and the staircase upward.

choices.text: Open the West Door — Den of Wolves
choices.consequence: You pull the heavy western door open.

choices.text: Pass Through the Archway — Dining Room
choices.consequence: You walk south under the carved archway.
You begin climbing the red marble stairs.

scenes.dmNotes: Let the door slam moment land. Pause after it. Let the players feel trapped before you describe anything else. The house is beautiful in the way that some predators are beautiful — superficially appealing, deeply wrong. The key design tone for the first floor is: PRESERVED. Everything is too perfect, too clean, for a house that's supposedly been abandoned. Something has been maintaining this place. Do not explain that. Let it unsettle.

scenes.title: Den of Wolves
scenes.subtitle: Ground Floor, Area 3

narrationBlocks.text: A hunter's den, or what was one. Dark oak walls, cold fireplace, mounted game. Three stuffed wolves are positioned around the room with a taxidermist's skill — crouched, alert, heads slightly lowered. Their glass eyes catch your light and hold it. They are looking at the fireplace. All three of them. Arranged around it as though in observation of something that once burned there.

A heavy mahogany table between two armchairs has a cask of dark wine, two wooden goblets, a pipe rack with three pipes still loaded, and a candlestick burned down to a waxy stub. The wine in the cask is still liquid. The ashes in the closest pipe are still gray, not black with age. Someone was here recently enough that these things haven't dried.
The room smells of old pipe tobacco, dried pine resin, and something beneath those things — faint, sweet, wrong. Like spoiled meat left in the cold.

DC 10 Perception — Looking at the wolves:

SUCCESS: The wolves are all pointed at something specific — not toward the hearth generally, but toward the fireplace's left corner. A slight crumbling of mortar there. A seam.

DC 13 Investigation — Examining the fireplace ashes:

SUCCESS: The ashes contain remnants of paper — partially burned sheets, dense with handwritten text. Most is illegible, but you can make out fragments: '...offerings made in the name of...' and '...the Eye that does not close...' and what appears to be '...our lord whose hand reaches from the grave...' 

None of this refers to Strahd.

DC 13 Investigation — Examining the chess set on the table:

SUCCESS: It is a fine ivory-and-obsidian set. The black pieces are carved normally. The white pieces are all missing their faces — smoothly blank where features should be. The white king piece is not blank: it is carved as a small hand with a single eye in its palm, lidless, staring up from the board.

A character with Religious knowledge (DC 11 Religion, passive counts) recognizes this: the Hand with the Eye is associated with Vecna, the Lich-God, the Whispered One. It is an Underdark cult symbol rarely seen in the Sword Coast.

OPTIONAL ENCOUNTER — WOLVES (only run if players specifically attack or desecrate the wolves):

The three stuffed wolves are exactly what they appear — taxidermied, dead. But the house can animate them if players are destructive or attempting to use them as cover/weapons. Standard Wolf statblocks, but their attacks feel wrong — too coordinated for beasts, too purposeful.

Loot from den cabinets:
• East cabinet (locked, DC 15 Thieves' Tools): A heavy crossbow, a hand crossbow, a light crossbow, and 20 bolts for each.
• North cabinet (unlocked): A small box of playing cards — ordinary — and eight crystal wine glasses. One glass has a faint inscription at the base: 'To the Knowing One's glory.'
• Wine cask: Drinkable, dark, earthy. A character with Poisoner's Kit or Herbalism DC 12 can detect trace amounts of a sleep-inducing herb — not dangerous in this quantity, but present. Someone was drugging their guests.

VECNA HOOK — CHESS PIECE:

Mark in your notes: any character who handles the white king chess piece feels a faint, rhythmic warmth — like a pulse — under their fingertips. It lasts only a moment and cannot be reproduced by re-touching the piece. This is the first in-person Vecna resonance. Do not explain it. Do not have a character explain it. Just note that it happens and file it.
The only exit is the door back to the main hall.

choices.consequence: You step back into the foyer.

scenes.dmNotes: This is a quiet room — no immediate combat, no trap. Its job is to be beautiful and wrong. The wolves, the drugged wine, the burned papers, the Vecna chess piece. Every single detail in this room points at a wealthy, comfortable family that was also something much, much worse. Let players take their time. This is a lore room.

scenes.title: Kitchen and Pantry
scenes.subtitle: Ground Floor, Area 4

narrationBlocks.text: The kitchen is tidy, which is wrong. Pots hang clean on their hooks. The worktable has been scrubbed. Flour and dried herbs are stored in labeled glass jars behind the counter. An iron dome oven stands near the east wall, cold now but with no sign of the years of use you'd expect on a working oven — no grease, no carbon buildup, no blackened crust at the rim.

A pantry door stands ajar to one side. Inside: bread that does not have mold on it. Potatoes that are not wrinkled. A string of dried sausages that smell the way sausages are supposed to smell. In a house that has supposedly been abandoned long enough for the children in the street to be centuries-dead, every piece of food in this kitchen is fresh.
It smells of kitchen heat and baking bread. Warm, domestic, utterly false. Like a trap baited with comfort.

THE FOOD:

Any character who eats the food — anything from the pantry, anything in the kitchen — let them swallow, let them start to describe how it tastes, and then tell them:

The taste changes mid-swallow. What was bread becomes something gray and cold. It tastes of wet grave dirt and old ash. Their body tries to reject it — a Retching Roll: DC 12 Constitution or the character is Incapacitated for 1 round from the reflex. The food provides no nourishment, no healing, no sustenance. But it doesn't damage them.

Note to DM: This is the house being cruel in a petty way. It presents comfort and then robs it.

DC 13 Investigation — Examining the flour on the worktable:

SUCCESS: There is a handprint in the flour. Child-sized. The print is fresh — the flour hasn't even settled back into it yet. It leads from the table toward the dumbwaiter in the southwest corner. The print has five fingers and is clean — no calluses, no roughness. This was a small child who is not currently visible.

THE DUMBWAITER:

A 2-foot wooden box on a rope-and-pulley in the southwest corner. A button on the wall next to it rings a tiny bell in the servants' room above (Area 7). The shaft connects to Area 7 on the second floor and Area 12 (the master suite) on the third.

A Small creature can squeeze into the box with a DC 10 Acrobatics check. The rope mechanism can support 200 lbs before breaking.

If a player uses it to travel: the journey up is slow, creaking, and in complete darkness. At any floor, pushing the box wall reveals the landing. If a player goes to the third floor (master suite), they emerge into an empty room and can catch a DC 13 Investigation check to see the journal mentioning the nursemaid's name.
A swinging door on the north wall leads to the dining room.

choices.consequence: You push through the swinging door northward.
You head back through the hall.

scenes.dmNotes: The food trick is the right kind of horrible — it is not dangerous, it is just deeply unpleasant and disorienting. Feed it to the character who seems most likely to eat something ("I check if the food is fresh" → "Yes, it appears fresh" → watches them eat it). The child handprint in the flour is meant to create unease — where is that child now? Answer: the ghost children left it when they passed through the kitchen intangibly. Players don't need to know that.

scenes.title: Dining Room
scenes.subtitle: Ground Floor, Area 5

narrationBlocks.text: A dining room for a family that wanted to appear more than it was. The mahogany table seats eight — its surface polished to a dark mirror — and the eight settings that remain are perfect: crystal glasses, silver-plate cutlery, porcelain dishes with a windmill pattern at their rims. Everything is set as if for a dinner party that is two minutes from beginning. And everything is wrong.

The crystal glasses have the faintest ring of old dried liquid at their bases. The silver has tarnished at its edges into brown. The porcelain dishes have infinitely fine hairline cracks following the windmill pattern like fault lines in something that was shaken very hard once and never properly healed. A crystal chandelier hangs above, unlit, the crystals giving back no light at all — absorbing it instead, somehow.

The smell here is harder to place. Beneath the furniture polish and dust, something older. A smell you would not expect in a dining room. Rust, and copper, and something organic that has been here long enough to stop actively smelling and just become part of the room.

DC 15 Perception — Examining the silverware closely:

SUCCESS: The tarnish pattern on each piece of silverware is wrong. Tarnish spreads from handling, from use, from fingerprints and oils. But the tarnish on these pieces forms faces. Small, smeared, agonized faces — the same face repeated, or many different ones, you can't tell. When you look away and look back they may have moved slightly. May have.

DC 12 Investigation — Examining the tapestry:

SUCCESS: The tapestry shows a hunting scene — riders in formal dress, hounds, a wolf being driven toward a cliff. The riders are distinctly portrayed: a wide man (Gustav?), a narrow woman (Elisabeth?), two smaller figures (Rose and Thorn?), and — partially obscured by the tapestry's fold — a fifth rider you can't see clearly. In the woven pond at the tapestry's bottom corner, none of the riders cast reflections.

DC 14: The wolf they are hunting has been cornered not by the hunters but by the hounds. The hunters are watching. They are not ending the hunt. They are... feeding something.

DC 13 Investigation — The sideboard cabinet:

SUCCESS: Behind the cracked plates and cloudy glasses: a carving knife, real and functional (treat as a Dagger). Also: a stack of ivory calling cards with the Durst family crest. These are for leaving at houses during formal visits. On the bottom of the stack, someone has written across several cards in different handwriting: 'He Sees All.' 'Vecna Waits.' 'His Eye, Our Offering.' None of the handwriting matches.

ATMOSPHERE DELIVERY NOTES:

This room is the upper class nightmare version of the horror. It looks expensive. It looks formal. It looks like a family that had money, manners, and a good tailor. And underneath all of that is something deeply wrong that the trappings of wealth couldn't paper over.

If players are quiet in here: let them feel the silence. If they're talking: let them. Then, clearly and without warning or drama, just describe: 'One of the crystal glasses shifts exactly a quarter-inch across its plate without sound and stops. Nothing else moves.'
The swinging door to the kitchen is south. The archway back to the main hall is north.

choices.consequence: You step back under the carved archway.
You push through the swinging door.

scenes.dmNotes: USE THE CALLING CARDS. If players find them and read "His Eye, Our Offering" and "Vecna Waits" — do not confirm or explain. Just let it sit in the room with them. This is one of the clearest signs the Dursts were Vecna cultists, not Strahd cultists, but resist the urge to underline it. The calling cards are a perfect, quiet horror detail. The ghost glass moving — use that if the scene needs a jolt. Deliver it flat, no buildup.

scenes.title: Upper Hall
scenes.subtitle: Second Floor, Area 6

narrationBlocks.text: The staircase delivers you to a wide, carpeted hallway of the second floor. The red-and-gold runner underfoot muffles your steps completely. Oil lamps in wall sconces are unlit, but the wick-stains suggest they were lit often. Heavy velvet drapes divide the hall from a narrow alcove at the far end — dark behind them, the darkness very still.

Two suits of plate armor flank the hallway, standing at attention beside their respective doors. Both helms are forged into snarling wolf faces — jaws open, teeth prominent, eye sockets dark and empty. Both suits hold halberds angled inward at 45 degrees, the blades meeting in an X that spans the corridor if you tried to pass between them.

It is colder here than the ground floor. Noticeably. Not the cold of poor insulation — the stone walls are thick. Something is drawing heat out of this hallway specifically. Your breath doesn't mist, but it almost should.

At the hallway's center, a large family portrait hangs in a gilt frame darkened with age. The Durst family, formally posed: a heavyset man with an air of authority, a narrow-faced woman in a high-collared gown, two children standing with the rigid discomfort of children who have been told many times not to fidget. The man holds a swaddled infant in the crook of his arm.

DC 14 Perception — Studying the portrait carefully:

SUCCESS: The composition of every family portrait places parents facing their children, or everyone facing outward. This one is different: the father faces forward, the children look toward the father, and the mother looks at neither. Her eyes are aimed with absolute precision at the infant he holds. Her expression is not love or pride or anxiety. It is contempt. Pure and cold and painted with careful craft by someone who either did not notice or did not care to flatter her.

Also: in the background of the painting, barely visible and almost obscured by the formal drape, there is a fifth door — one that does not correspond to any door in the hallway you are standing in.

DC 12 Investigation — Examining the armor suits:

SUCCESS: The suits are occupied. Not by creatures — by something preserved inside. The joint seams bleed when pressed: not fresh blood, but something thicker and darker that smells of old iron. The halberds are functional and could be taken (reach weapon, 1d10 slashing). The armor itself is fused from years of the house's peculiar preservation — useless as equipment.

If a character tries to force the armor out of their path: each suit weighs approximately 450 lbs and will not yield. They have no apparent mechanism that can be activated from the outside.

ARMOR RULE FOR THIS FLOOR:

The wolf armor does NOT animate on the second floor. That happens on the third. The second-floor suits are locked in place and function purely as environmental dread — heavy, watching, full of something dead.

If players attack them: they take 6 damage before announcing: 'The armor shudders when struck but not with vibration — with something that feels like surprise, like being woken up. Its head turns slowly to look at whoever struck it. It does not move toward you. It just looks.'

If they take the halberds: they work normally. The suits don't protest.

SECOND FLOOR CONNECTIONS:
• North door (behind armor) → Servants' Room (Area 7)
• South door → Library (Area 8)
• East door → Conservatory (Area 10)
• Stairway → Third Floor (Area 11)
Doors lead to the Servants' Room (north), the Library (south), and the Conservatory (east). The staircase continues up to the third floor.

choices.consequence: You descend back to the ground floor.
You edge past the wolf helm and try the northern door.
You open the eastern door.
You open the southern door.
You continue up the staircase.

scenes.dmNotes: The portrait is one of the best moments in this house. Pause after describing the mother's expression. Let it sink in. If players ask what she is looking at: "The baby." The tone of that answer should tell them everything about what kind of mother Elisabeth Durst was. The wolf armor paranoia isn't resolved here — it pays off on Floor 3.

scenes.title: Servants' Room
scenes.subtitle: Second Floor, Area 7

narrationBlocks.text: A plain, undecorated room. Two narrow beds with wool blankets folded tight at their corners. A small table between them with a stub candle and an unlit lamp. Pressed servant uniforms are draped over the bed frames — ironed, buttoned to the collar, ready for a body to step into them. The boots are gone.

Unlike the rest of the house, this room has no pretense. It was functional, it served, and it was abandoned with the domestic urgency of people who left in the middle of a task they didn't get to finish.

DC 11 Investigation — Looking under the beds or inside the mattress seams:

SUCCESS: Under the left mattress: a small handmade cloth wallet containing 3 sp and a folded letter, written in a cramped, careful hand: 'Mia — Do not go in the basement when the candles are lit. I mean it. Whatever the Mister and Missus do down there is not our concern and God help you if you make it yours. Burn this. — T'

The letter is not burned. Whether Mia listened or not, you have no way of knowing.

DUMBWAITER:

A wooden box on a rope-and-pulley in the northwest corner. Press the button on the wall beside it and a small bell rings in the kitchen below. The shaft connects to the kitchen (Area 4) and to an access point beside the master suite (Area 12) on the third floor.

A Small creature can ride it. A Medium creature can attempt to squeeze: DC 12 Acrobatics, failure means they get stuck for 1 round before the box returns to where it started.

Potential uses:
• A familiar can travel between floors via the dumbwaiter shaft
• A Small character can reconnoiter the master suite before the party arrives
• Climbing the rope instead of using the box: DC 13 Athletics

choices.consequence: You step back out into the hall past the wolf armor.

scenes.dmNotes: The letter is a small, human horror. Two servants. One is trying to warn the other. The warning was not heeded. Leave the players to sit with that. Do not give this scene more than 5 minutes — it is a breather and a lore crumb.

scenes.title: Library
scenes.subtitle: Second Floor, Area 8

narrationBlocks.text: Floor-to-ceiling shelves wrap three walls, packed with hundreds of heavy volumes. A mahogany desk sits in the center, positioned to face the door — whoever worked here liked to see who was entering. A red leather high-back chair faces the desk. The lamp above the desk is iron, elegant, unlit. They spent money on this room. Spent significant money.

Every book on every shelf is perfectly upright. Spine out, precisely placed, alphabetized in Old Common. Whoever did this was meticulous. Or obsessive. Or both. Every book except one: a fat red tome on the middle shelf, slightly out of alignment, its spine worn smooth at eye level where fingers have found it again and again.
Old paper and dried ink. Beneath that: faint sulfur, the residue of a room where certain kinds of texts have been read many times over many years. This is not a reading room. This is a workroom.

DC 12 Investigation — Examining the books generally:

SUCCESS: Most are legitimate academic texts: natural philosophy, history, cartography, heraldry, architecture. But the subjects cluster around a specific period of Pre-Spellplague history — specifically works relating to arcanist death cults of the Eastern Underdark. There are also several texts on the anatomic differences between living and undead tissue. These books are annotated in multiple hands, as if they were studied by several people.

DC 14 Investigation — Examining the red book specifically:

SUCCESS: 'The Anatomy of Beasts' — a legitimate natural history text on the surface. The shelf shows fresh scuff marks where the book has been pulled forward hundreds of times. If pulled: the entire shelf section swings inward on a hidden pivot, revealing the Secret Room (Area 9). The mechanism is well-oiled — completely silent.
On the desk: a heavy iron key with a wolf-head bow. It fits the padlocked door to the Children's Room in the attic (Area 20).

DESK CONTENTS — If searched:

• Top drawer: dried ink, two quill pens, a blank sheaf of parchment.
• Bottom drawer (stuck, DC 10 Strength): a brass paperweight in the shape of a hand holding an eye — clearly a Vecna cult object. Worth 15 gp as a curiosity; 45 gp if sold to the right collector who knows what it is.
• On the desk surface: a half-filled logbook with entries noting dates, names, and amounts. Some entries read: 'Offering received. 6 silver, 2 cp.' and 'Two more swear the Oath.' The last entry is dated and the ink is smeared as if the writer was hurried: 'The Eye accepts. It is done. Walter is —' It ends there.

VECNA LOG KEY:

The 'Eye' in the logbook is the Eldritch Eye — the artifact the party will find on Delvin's body in the dungeon. The Dursts were not Strahd's servants. They were Vecna's. They were placed here through Strahd's domain by Vecna's influence, tasked with building a cell. The Eye was meant to be delivered to a greater collector. It was not.
The secret door is behind the red book. The only other exit is back to the upper hall.

choices.consequence: You leave the library.

choices.text: Pull the Red Book → Secret Room
choices.consequence: The shelf swings inward without a sound. Cold air exhales from beyond.

scenes.dmNotes: MAKE SURE THE KEY IS FOUND. Players who miss the attic key will face a lockpick bottleneck later. If they search the desk, they find it. If they don't search the desk by the time they reach the attic, feel free to have one player notice it glinting under the desk lamp or have it visible in a DC 10 Perception check. It is too important to miss.

scenes.title: Secret Room
scenes.subtitle: Second Floor, Area 9

narrationBlocks.text: The shelf opens onto a room with no windows, no decoration, and no pretense. The smell hits immediately: sulfur, old blood, and the particular sharpness of preserved things in a sealed space. Shelves hold grimoires bound in what you would rather not identify as leather. Iron brackets line the walls, the rings and chains hanging from them long since gone cold and still.

A figure in black robes is slumped over a small writing desk in the far corner. Not dramatically — they have simply ceased to be upright, their weight settling forward over years until their forehead rests on the desk surface. Their hands still grip a parchment. Their flesh has long dried and gone tight. This person did not leave.
The cold here is specific. Not the general cold of the second floor hallway. This is the cold of a room where something happened that cannot be taken back, and the space remembers it.

DC 13 Medicine or Investigation — Examining the skeleton:

SUCCESS: This person died of thirst, over a period of no less than a week. There are no wounds. Nothing killed them except being sealed in a room with no exit — the secret door only opens from the library side. The door they used to enter is not present in this room. They were locked in from outside and chose to write rather than beat on the wall.

The parchment they clutch is from Strahd. Read aloud immediately after describing this.

My most pathetic servant,

I am not a messiah. I am not a god waiting to repay devotion. You are not missionaries. You are not chosen ones. You are worms writhing in my earth, and your underground games and your little eye-and-hand prayers are an amusement that has grown tiresome.

You reached out to me. You offered. I did not respond. The correct lesson is silence, not repeat correspondence.

If you write again, I will stop ignoring you.

— S.Z.V.
narrationBlocks.speaker: The Letter (signed by Strahd von Zarovich)
narrationBlocks.emotion: Elegant penmanship. Ice-cold register. Written with the absolute economy of someone who has never in their life needed to raise their voice to be frightening.

narrationBlocks.text:
LETTER CONTEXT:

This is critical campaign lore. The Dursts were Vecna cultists trying to gain Strahd's patronage as a secondary power. Strahd refused them entirely. They died here not because of Strahd but despite him — their devotion to Vecna ultimately consumed them in ways Strahd never needed to engineer.

The skeleton is not Gustav Durst. Gustav became a ghast in the dungeon. This is a tertiary cultist — a priest or acolyte who was locked in here as punishment for sending the letter without permission and then simply... never let out.
An iron-bound chest in the corner contains the party's most significant finds in the house above the dungeon.
narrationBlocks.lootDetails: Cloak of Protection (+1 AC & saves, attunement) • 4x Potion of Healing • Chain Shirt • Silver Shortsword • Iron Gate Key (unlocks dungeon Area 24 gate)

narrationBlocks.text:
CHEST DETAILS:

• Lock: DC 15 Thieves' Tools to pick. Alternatively, AC 15, 20 HP to break.
• Cloak of Protection: Gives +1 to AC and saving throws while attuned. Worth giving to whoever needs it most.
• Silver Shortsword: Functions as a magic weapon for purposes of overcoming resistances; useful against the undead ahead.
• Iron Gate Key: THIS IS CRITICAL. It opens the iron gate in the dungeon (Area 24). Players who miss this key face DC 16 picking or DC 20 forcing to proceed past that chokepoint. Make sure someone picks this up.

Books on the shelves: include texts in Abyssal and Infernal, one in an entirely unknown script. Reading them requires 8 hours and a DC 15 Arcana; results in a temporary madness. Do not encourage players to read them deeply during the session.
